concept.logline: A rigged 1974 wheel shows how the first number you see bends your guess.
concept.central_question: Why does a random number change your answer?
concept.claim: In 1974 a rigged wheel moved people's estimates by 20 points; the effect replicates, though for prices the evidence is mixed.

scenes.narration: In 1974, two psychologists rigged a wheel.
It could only stop on two numbers.
scenes.graphic: Photo: asset:P0007 | push | A gambling wheel | illustrative
Photo: asset:P0008 | pan-right | Only two numbers ever came up | illustrative

scenes.narration: Then people guessed what share of UN members are African.
scenes.graphic: Photo: asset:P0008 | pull | Guess. How much of the UN is African? | illustrative

scenes.narration: After a 10, the middle guess was 25 percent. After 65, it was 45.
scenes.graphic: Chart: 25 vs 45 | after a 10, after a 65

scenes.narration: A meaningless number moved the answer.
Big replications since have found the same pull.
scenes.graphic: Timeline: 1974 the rigged wheel → 2014 many labs repeat it | It held

scenes.narration: With prices, researchers say the evidence is mixed.
scenes.graphic: Steps: First number → Your guess → Your price? | At the till: the evidence is mixed

scenes.narration: So ask: who picked the first number?
